An ACID is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (H+) in solution.

Read the following paragraph and highlight the key terms to help you answer the questions that
follow.
All energy forms can be separated into one of two categories: potential energy (stored energy)
or kinetic energy (energy that moving objects have). Therefore, electrical energy (which is
due to moving charges), light energy (which is due to the movement of electromagnetic
waves), sound energy (due to motion of compressional waves through a medium) and heat
energy (due to the vibration and movement of particles) are actually all forms of kinetic
energy. What we generally call kinetic energy could be described more precisely as
macroscopic motion energy. On the other hand, gravitational, elastic, chemical and nuclear
energy are all forms of potential energy.

PART 2: CALCULATIONS IN CHEMISTRY
CHAPTER 9: Atomic, Molecular and Formula Mass

The term MOLECULAR MASS was previously referred to as molecular weight (or formula weight). It is used for all substances even though some do not exist in molecular
form. The term FORMULA MASS (FM) will be used in this book to avoid this possible
confusion.

ATOMIC MASS
In Science it is often necessary to be able to express the mass of an atom. Each atom
has a mass of approximately 10-23kg (0.000 000 000 000 000 000 000 01 kg). Masses
of atoms in common units (e.g. in kg) are too small to be of practical value hence a
relative scale has been devised.
The mass of atoms is expressed using a scale which defines the mass of one atom of
the carbon -12 (12C) isotope to be exactly 12 atomic mass units.
The average value obtained on this scale for the mass of one atom of an element is
termed the RELATIVE ATOMIC MASS of the element.
Relative Atomic Mass (which will be referred to simply as Atomic Mass) was
previously referred to as Atomic Weight.
The (RELATIVE) ATOMIC MASS of an element is the ratio of the average mass of an
atom of that element to one-twelfth of the mass of one atom of the carbon -12 isotope.
Atomic Mass (AM) -

Average mass of one atom of the element
One twelfth mass of one atom of carbon -12

NOTE: 1. Atomic Mass is a ratio of masses hence it has NO units.
2. As naturally occurring elements generally contain several isotopes, the
average mass of an atom compared to one twelfth mass of a carbon -12
atom will produce a ratio which will not be an exact whole number.
However, most of the atomic masses given inside the front cover have
been rounded to whole numbers.

DETERMINATION OF FORMULA MASS
For any substance (element or compound ), the formula mass is a sum of the atomic
masses of EACH atom making up the formula of the substance.
The Table of Atomic Masses found inside the cover has been used for all Type Examples and Answers to problems in this book.
TYPE EXAMPLE 1: Find the formula mass of oxygen (gas).
Formula: 02
FM(02) = 2 x AM(O)
= 2 x 16
= 32
i.e. Formula mass of oxygen (gas) is 32.
TYPE EXAMPLE 2: What is the formula mass of sulfur dioxide?
Formula : SO2
FM(SO) = AM(S) + 2 X AM(O)
= 32 + 2(16)
= 64
i.e. Formula mass of sulfur dioxide is 64.

MOLECULAR MASS, FORMULA MASS
The mass of a molecule of an element or compound can be expressed in similar
terms to that used for masses of atoms . The term used is RELATIVE MOLECULAR
MASS (or simply MOLECULAR MASS).
The MOLECULAR MASS is the ratio of the average mass of one molecule of a
substance to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon - 12 atom.
Molecular Mass =

Average mass of one molecule of substance
One twelfth mass of one atom of carbon -12

 The first choice has three options: Greater than one metre long; greater than
or equal to 500 millimetres long; and less than 500 millimetres long. The
remaining choices have only two choices, as in a normal dichotomous key.

This bird is 280–320 mm in length. It
has a distinctive black head with a
white collar. The eyes are dark
brown, the bill blue-grey with a
hooked tip, and the legs are black.

To identify this bird, start in the middle. Its length is less than 500 mm.
The next choice is whether the legs are black or not. This bird has black legs.
The choice for birds with black legs is whether the beak is hooked or not. This
bird has a hook on the end of the beak. It is a butcher bird.

searchText:
Genetic Variation
Label the following diagram

Humans have __ pairs of chromosomes in every cell. They exist in pairs
because you get ____ of them from your mother and half from your _______.
Egg cells and sperm cells are called gametes. Each gamete contains half of the
parents 46 chromosomes, one of each pair.
A gene is a section of DNA which codes for a specific characteristic e.g. hair
colour. Since we have two of each chromosome, we have two copies of each
gene, these are called alleles. You get one from each parent.
You can be homozygous; both alleles are the same or heterozygous where each
allele is different.
Some genes are dominant and some are recessive. A dominant gene always
expressed if present and a recessive gene only shows if there are two copies.
Your phenotype is a description of the characteristics that are shown.
Your genotype is a description of the exact combination of genes you have.
Brown hair (B) is dominant over blonde (b). If my phenotype is brown, I have
brown hair, my genotype could be Bb (heterozygous) or BB (homozygous).

 Worked example.
1. If a blonde person mated with a homozygous brown haired person
what would their off spring look like?
If one parent is blonde and blonde hair is RECESSIVE their genotype
must be bb meaning they carry two copies of the blonde allele b.
The other parent is homozygous; this means he also has both alleles the
same. His phenotype is brown hair, so his genotype is BB which means he
carries two copies of the brown allele B.

SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING

Plant tales
Are you aware that when you bite into an apple, cherry
or orange you are actually eating the enlarged ovary
of the plant? Did you know that these swollen ovaries
contain the plant’s ‘babies’ in their embryonic form? The
plants are using you as a way of distributing their ‘young’
out into the world.

Eggs, embryos, seeds and fruit

HOW ABOUT THAT!
Fruits that attract animals are
usually brightly coloured. When
a fruit is eaten by an animal,
only the soft parts of the fruit
are digested. The seeds are not
broken down inside the animal
and are passed out in its faeces.

Once the flower has done its job and the egg cell has been fertilised
by the pollen nucleus, another sequence of events takes place. The
fertilised egg, in the middle of the ovule, divides into a little ball of cells
that becomes an embryo. Special tissue called endosperm surrounds
the embryo and supplies it with food.

The ovule becomes the seed and tissue forms around it to provide
a protective seed coat. During the formation of the seed, the ovary
expands and turns into a fruit.

Seed dispersal
One of the main jobs that fruits do is to help disperse or spread the seeds.
There is a variety of ways in which plants disperse their seeds: dispersal
may involve animals, including birds (such as in tomatoes, grapes and
apples); water (such as in coconuts); or wind (such as in grasses and

For example, the fruits of some

split open suddenly when they are
ripe and dry, throwing the seeds
out for long distances.

germination
The embryo, inside the seed, is
made up of three different parts:
the baby shoot (plumule), the
baby root (radicle) and one or two
thick, wing-like cotyledons.

When the conditions are right,
the seed bursts open and a new
plant grows out. This process
is called germination. When
germination is complete, the
embryo has become a young
plant or seedling.
There are three environmental
conditions that are needed
by all seeds before they will
germinate: water, oxygen
and a certain temperature,

usually warm. Water is necessary
for the seed to swell and burst
open and then to transport food
to the growing embryo. Oxygen
is required to help provide the
energy needed for growth and
development. The temperature
varies with the particular

searchText:
Lesson 4: Up and Down in the Wild: Predator and Prey
Overview
This lesson allows students to explore the interactions of
two animal populations (wolves and moose) within an
ecosystem. One animal in the simulation is a predator.
The other animal is its prey. Their populations rise and
fall (oscillate) over time as they interact and impact one
another.
Learning Goals:
• Match predators with corresponding prey animals.
• Explore a population simulation with two interacting
populations.
• Represent and interpret data on a line graph.
• Tell the story of how and why two populations go up
and down (oscillate) over time.
• Identify predator/prey animals in ecosystems.

Lesson 4 – Level A – Ages 5+
Time:
Two-three 45-minute periods
Materials:
• One computer for every 2-3
students
•

Simulation online at http://
www.clexchange.org/curriculum/complexsystems/
oscillation/Oscillation_PredpreyA.asp

•

Handouts (See page 4-9)

Curricular Connections:
• Science: Populations,
ecosystems, scientific
method
•

Math: Representing and
interpreting data*

•

Reading: Describing
connections among ideas*

* Common Core Standards

Figure 1: Title Screen

Student Challenge
What settings for the moose and wolves create the most
stable populations, i.e., with the minimum fluctuation?

Key system dynamics concepts
and insights:
• Populations do not exist in
isolation; other factors (e.g.,
number of prey, amount
of food supply) affect their
growth and decline.
•

Predators and their prey
form a type of complex
system that can exhibit
oscillatory behavior.

Lesson 4 – Level A • UpDownWild • ©2012 Creative Learning Exchange • 1

 Lesson Details
Preparation:
1. Create groups of two to three students each.
2. Copy included handouts for each student or
student group. Make multiple copies of the
simulation record sheet, depending on how
many runs you’d like students to complete.
3. Cut or have students cut out animal
predators and prey cards (Handout 1).
4. Check computers to make sure you can
access the simulation.
Session 1:
1. Introduce vocabulary terms (predator, prey,
ecosystem, etc.) as needed.
2. Distribute card sets to student groups and
have them find matches for the different
predator/prey animals. Students can use the
T-chart on page 5 (Handout 2) to classify
their cards. Optional: Provide some blank
cards for students who would like to draw
additional animals. Students may come
up with varying answers. This is one set of
answers, based on the initial data used.

3. Briefly compare and discuss the different
matches. You may want to note that some
predators may have multiple food sources,
e.g., a coyote may eat rodents, rabbits, cats,
and other small mammals.

 Lesson Details
4. Show students the simulation in the classroom and
read the introduction together (Figures 2 and 3).
5. Have students work in their small groups to “Make
Decisions” (Figure 4). The simulation is initially
set, based on data for wolves and moose on a small
island. The moose is the main source of food for the
wolves.
6. Have students continue to “See What Happens”
(Figure 5), recording their data on Handout 3 on
page 6. After completing the initial run, students
can continue to explore, asking “What if ” questions
relating to the wolves and moose while using
additional copies of Handout 4 on page 7.
7. Students can also run the simulation for different
animals they have researched and record their data
on the simulation record sheet for each one. Note
that the simulation results may vary, including some
unrealistic results, if they input data that would not
make sense. An example would be an insect with a
long lifespan and lots of babies.
Session 2 and beyond:
1. If needed, have students complete the simulation
within their small groups.
2. After running the simulation multiple times, students
continue to the “Think About It” section (Figure 6).
3. Debrief the simulation experience using ideas for
bringing the lesson home and assessment (Handouts
5 and 6).

Bringing the Lesson Home:

It” section of the simulation within small groups
or as a class.

searchText:
CHAPTER 10: Transferring and transforming energy

Worksheet 10.1

Skateboard flick cards
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class: ................................................

Skate parks are designed to help skateboard
riders create the speed and elevation they need
to perform tricks. The half-pipe is a U-shaped
ramp joined by a flat section at the bottom. In
‘vert’ competitions, the half-pipe is entered
from a platform at the top of the ramp. The
rider gains speed as they move down the wall.
Professional skateboarders use the transfer of
energy during a vert manoeuvre to create more
‘airtime’ to perform tricks.
Many energy transformations occur during
vert skating in a half-pipe. While moving
downwards, a skater’s gravitational potential
energy begins to transform into kinetic energy.
At the bottom of the half-pipe, the skater has
maximum kinetic energy, but little to no
gravitational potential energy. The skater’s
kinetic energy at the bottom of the half-pipe is
equal to their original gravitational potential
energy at the top of the ramp. During the climb
up the opposite side of the half-pipe, the
skater’s kinetic energy begins to transform back
into gravitational potential energy. At the very

top of the climb, the kinetic energy will have
transformed back into gravitational potential energy.
If the skater begins at a certain height on one
side of the ramp, how can he or she launch into
the air more than four metres above the
original starting point?
By crouching going down the ramp and ‘pushing
off ’ near the bottom, the skater transfers some of
the energy stored in his or her leg muscles to the
system. Now, the skater can move higher than the
starting level and perform aerial tricks.
To show your understanding of the energy
transformations that occur during a vert manoeuvre,
create your own vert skating flick card set by
following these instructions.
1. Print and label each of the fourteen cards on the
next page with one of the following captions:
● gravitational potential energy
● gravitational potential energy transforming
into kinetic energy
● kinetic energy

Worksheet 10.1

Investigating neurons
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class: ...........................................

The nervous system is made up of billions and billions of neurons. A neuron is an individual nerve
cell that transmits information around the body, combining it with information from other sources.
Neurons have specialised functions. Some neurons specialise in transmitting information from
the sense organs and muscles to the CNS. Other neurons specialise in sending information to the
organs, muscles or glands from the CNS. Some neurons carry information between neurons.
The number of neurons in the human body is not known. However, estimates of the number of
neurons in the human brain alone range from 10 billion to about 100 billion neurons. The entire
nervous system that extends throughout the body is comprised of neurons that connect with many
other neurons to enable the continuous communication of information around the body. Unlike skin
cells, for example, the body does not replace neurons if they die. However, the function of a neuron,
if damaged, is often taken over by another neuron.
Not all neurons look the same. They vary in shape and size depending on where they are located
in the body and on their specific function. However, most neurons have some features in common.
The diagrams on this worksheet show the different types of neurons in the human body. They
also shows the various parts of each neuron.

Structure of the neuron
Soma: The soma is the large section located centrally in the neuron. The soma, or cell body, is the
structure that determines whether the neuron will be activated and thus transmit (send) messages to
other neurons.
Within the soma is the nucleus of the neuron. The nucleus contains the biochemical information
that provides the energy to keep the neuron functioning. The soma has a number of extensions that
branch from it. There are two main types of extensions — dendrites and axons. Some neurons have
thousands of dendrites that extend from the soma, but most neurons have only one axon.
Dendrite: A dendrite is a short, thin, widely branching nerve fibre that is specialised to detect
and receive neural information. Like an antenna, dendrites receive incoming information from other
neurons and transmit the information to the soma.
Axon: An axon is a single, tubelike, fluid-filled extension that transmits messages from the soma
to other cells in the body including other neurons, muscles, organs and glands. Most neurons have
only one axon.
Axons vary in length, for example, some axons extend over a metre from your spine to your big
toe, others are as small as the width of a single hair.
At the end of each axon are branches called axon terminals. Each axon terminal has a small
knob-like swelling at the tip of it called a synaptic knob or terminal button.
The synaptic knob is a small structure like a sack that stores chemicals called neurotransmitters
that assist in the transmission of neural information from one neuron to another. Axon terminals are
located physically close to dendrites of other neurons, enabling information to pass easily between
neurons as messages are transmitted to and from the CNS.

The role of neurons
There are three main types of neurons, each of which has a different role in the nervous system. The
three types of neurons are called sensory neurons, motor neurons and interneurons.
Sensory neurons and motor neurons are found primarily in the peripheral nervous system,
whereas interneurons are primarily found in the CNS.

Conductors are materials that readily allow electric charges to flow through them when a
voltage is applied across them. In the late 1800s it was discovered that it was the electrons from
the atoms making up the conductor that moved through the material and that the protons were
inside the nucleus and remained fixed in position.
Metals are good conductors of electrcity and non-metals are not. An exception to this is
graphite, a form of carbon that is a conductor. The conductivity of a metal decreases as the
temperature of that conductor increases. This is explained by the increase in resistance to the
flow of electrons through a conductor as it heats up. Resistance to electron flow is caused by
vibrations of the atoms hindering the flow of electrons through a material. As the temperature
increases the vibrations increase and so electron flow is reduced.
Non-metals are classified as insulators. When a voltage is applied across the ends of an insulator
almost no current flows as the electrons are not free to move through the material. If electrical
charges are transferred to one location on an insulator, they remain there and do not move about.
Insulators are important as they are used in electric circuits to prevent us making direct contact
with current-carrying wires and so preventing electrocution.

TOPIC 11: Forensics

Worksheet 11.3

Read my lips
Answers
The study of lip prints is called celioscopy. A person’s lip prints are unique. The use of lip prints in
criminal cases is limited because the credibility of lip prints has not been firmly established in our
courts.
The following is a case where the crime scene is a school bathroom. The crime is graffiti and
the court is the principal’s office.

A student at the school has been writing graffiti in lipstick on the girls’
bathroom mirror. She has been signing her work with her lip print. The
cleaner has to clean the mirror several times every day to remove the graffiti
and is getting tired of this prank. The principal has each of the 5 suspects
seen leaving the restroom make her lip print on a piece of card to compare to
the lip print on the bathroom mirror. The girls are then taken to the bathroom
where the cleaner shows how to clean off the lipstick by using the toilet
brush!

identify the culprit.

Mystery in the house
Answers
You are a forensic scientist within your own home. You have your forensic toolbox with you. Turn
a room of your home into a crime scene and decide the type of crime that has been committed.
Design a crime scene investigator’s report that outlines the steps you would take to investigate
the evidence in this room.

1. How would you seal off the room?
Close and lock doors and windows, post a look out.

2. How would you investigate what has happened in this room before you arrived?
Careful observation and measurement

wrong position or a glass left on a table. How would you record this evidence?
Photography, sketches

type of hair or fibre?
Tweezers and plastic sample bags, labelled containers
.........................................................................................................................................................

Glass or metal surfaces, crockery, cutlery or cooking utensils, doorknobs, windows, mirrors etc.
.........................................................................................................................................................
.........................................................................................................................................................
6. Is there any evidence that you cannot see in the daylight? How would you identify this
evidence?
Ultraviolet and infra-red lighting may detect blood, fingerprints or fibres.

CHAPTER 11: Forensics

Worksheet 11.5

Forensics: Summary
Answers
Fill in the gaps.
1. evidence: anything that assists with a conclusion or judgement — that is, a testimony or
material sample
2. accelerant: a substance, such as petrol, that is used to start a fire or explosion
3. database: an organised collection of data, arranged for easy and speedy retrieval
4. analyse: examine closely to answer a question or solve a problem
5. psychology: the science of mental processes, particularly emotional and behavioural
characteristics. Practitioners are not medically trained and do not prescribe medicine.
6. Botanist: a scientist who studies the life of plants
7. Whorl: a circular type of fingerprint pattern
8. Cuticle: the scaly outer covering of a hair
9. Magnifying glass: a convex lens used to enlarge an object
10. Administration: the management of an organisation, business or task to meet certain goals
11. Psychiatrist: a medically trained doctor who studies the mental condition and behaviour of
patients
12. Pollen: a fine coarse powder produced by seed plants
13. Comparison microscope: a microscope that allows two objects to be viewed at the same time
so they can be compared
14. Liability: an obligation, responsibility, hindrance or something that causes a disadvantage
Write definitions for the following terms.
1. civil court: a law court that hears legal matters, usually minor, and not relating to a criminal
investigation — for example, child custody battles.

2. fibres: fine threads that make up fabric and paper
3. entomologist: a scientist who studies insects
4. counterfeit: an imitation or copy that is made to deliberately deceive; for example, counterfeit
money

5. trace evidence the tiny evidence found at crime scenes — includes hair, fibres and soil

social and cultural developments?

CHAPTER 3: Cells

Worksheet 3.1

History of the light
microscope
Answers
Read the following text and answer the questions that follow.
Before the invention of the microscope, biologists did not know
that living things were made of cells. The first light microscopes
were built from spectacle lenses and tubes by Zaccharias Janssen
and his father Hans in Holland between 1590 and 1610. In 1665,
Robert Hooke used a simple microscope that magnified by 30
to observe thin slices of cork. He found structures that reminded
him of the boxes or cells of a honeycomb, and so he called them
cells.
He examined other plant tissue in later experiments and
observed that some of these cells contained a fluid. In the 1670s
and 1680s Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using a single lens
microscope, observed cellular life forms (or protozoa) in sea
water and rainwater. He identified microbes such as yeast and
bacteria. His lenses were superior to those of Hooke because he
had trained as a lens grinder and polisher. Magnifications of
about 270 were achieved due to the great radius of curvature
of his lenses. (The radius of curvature of a lens is a measure of
how curved it is.)
It was not until the middle of the nineteenth century that
significant improvements were made to optical microscopes so
that greater magnification and resolution could be achieved. The
American Charles Spencer developed a company that produced
light microscopes with magnification up to 1250. By using
blue light, the magnification was increased to 5000.
Throughout the twentieth century, further improvements in lens
manufacture, improving contrast and the use of specialised dyes
to stain tissue led to improved images of living matter.

Transpiration
1. Consider the following two diagrams of the surface of a green leaf.

(a) Two stomates are shown. Explain why the stomatal pore at the left is open more widely than
the one on the right.
The stomate on the left is more open as it is actively transpiring. The other stomate is closed
as the plant could be under water stress.

(b) Define the term ‘transpiration’ in your own words.
Transpiration is the loss of water from a plant through its stomates. The transpiration stream
draws water from the roots, up the stem and into the leaves.

(c) A student performed an experiment to measure the rate of transpiration using a bean seedling.
She used the apparatus shown below.
(i) The student decided to place a thin layer of olive oil on the water surface
before the experiment began. Explain why she did this.
To prevent evaporation from the water surface so she could see how the
water level dropped due to transpiration alone

(ii) Explain how the student will measure the rate of transpiration.
Mark a scale on the side of the vessel. Measure the water level on this
scale as a function of time.

Density of stomates
2. A student wanted to find out if there are more stomates on the top or the bottom surface of a leaf.
She painted the bottom surface of a small section of a leaf with nail polish. When the nail polish
was dry she peeled it off and observed it under the microscope. She could see imprints of the
stomates in the layer of nail polish.
(a) Explain what the student will need to do next. (Remember that she wants to find out if there
are more stomates on the top or bottom of the leaf.) Paint the top surface of a small section of
the leaf with nail polish. Allow to dry and peel off the nail polish; then observe under the
microscope as before..

density of stomates, i.e. how many stomates there are per cm2 of leaf. Explain why this is
necessary. The layer of nail polish peeled off the top and bottom surfaces may have different
areas. She needs to control this variable. By counting how many stomates there are per
square centimetre, she is ensuring that she compares the same area for the top and bottom
surface.

(c) The student finds that there is a much greater density of stomates on the bottom surface of the

Many animals eat more than one type of food. This means that they are in more than one food

web. Note that some animals, such as the seagull, may actually be in more than one level,
depending on which chain you follow to the top. A food web also has decomposers. Decomposers
are organisms, such as bacteria, worms and fungi, that break down dead animals and plants. The
nutrients in the dead animals and plants are recycled back into the food web.

Carnivores, such as the dog whelk, that eat first-order consumers are known as second-order
consumers. The seagull is a third-order consumer because it eats the second-order consumer.

searchText:
CHAPTER 4: Systems — living connections

Worksheet 4.4

Breathing — constructing
a report
Answers
Use the information in your textbook together with other information from the internet and library
to complete a scaffold about the topic ‘Breathing’.
Use the completed scaffold to write a final report using a word processing application. Include
labelled diagrams to show the processes of inhalation and exhalation.
Title: Breathing
Heading: Introduction
Make general statements about:
● the name and location of the respiratory organs in the body

lungs (in chest cavity); trachea (links nasal cavity to lung bronchi); bronchi (tubes leading
into lungs); diaphragm (muscle to change volume of chest cavity)
●

the differences between inhalation and exhalation.

Inhalation: breathing in (richer in oxygen/poorer in carbon dioxide)
Exhaling: breathing out (less rich in oxygen/increased amounts of carbon dioxide)
Heading: Structure of the respiratory system
Record information about:
● lungs

Two lungs; composed of many alveoli
●

bronchi

●

Two tubes; divides into smaller tubes called bronchioles
trachea
Tube that takes air from nasal cavity down into the bronchi. Wall has cartilage for strength.

●

diaphragm.

Muscular tissue that separates chest from abdomen. Contracts and expands and adjusts
air pressure inside chest cavity. Works with lungs to help move air in and out

Heading: Alveoli and blood capillaries
Record information about:
● the structure of alveoli

Small air sacs (resemble bunches of grapes) at the ends of small bronchioles
●

the connection between alveoli and blood capillaries.

The surface of each alveolus is covered with capillaries so that gases can be exchanged
quickly with the bloodstream.

Heading: Conclusion
Make a statement about the importance of inhalation and exhalation to the health of the body.

Inhalation brings fresh air and oxygen into the body and exhalation removes carbon dioxide waste.
If either system is unhealthy due to smoking or disease, then the process is less efficient and
affects the health of the whole body.

searchText:
Worksheet 5.6

Corrosion and combustion
Answers
Corrosion
1. Corrosion is a process in which a metal or alloy is attacked by agents such as air and water,
leading to the degradation and destruction of the material. The following diagrams compare the
corrosion of iron and aluminium.
(a) As both metals are attacked, oxide layers form on the
surface. The iron oxide is called rust. Use your
knowledge of the activity series of metals to predict
which metal (Fe or Al) will react with air and water
more rapidly.
Al as it is higher in the activity series than Fe.

(b) Iron continues to rust whereas aluminium stops
corroding. Explain why this happens.
The iron oxide (rust) layer is porous. Oxygen and
water continue to penetrate through the rust layer to
attack the iron beneath. This does not happen with
aluminium oxide as the corrosion layer on the surface
is non-porous.

(c) Name a metal that is used to coat iron to prevent it from rusting.
Zinc (process = galvanising)
.................................................................................................................................................

Combustion
2. In combustion reactions a substance reacts with oxygen and releases energy. The energy
released can be in the form of heat, light and sometimes sound. The following diagram shows
the blue flame of a Bunsen burner.
(a) The Bunsen burner uses natural gas, which is mainly
methane. Write the chemical formula for methane.
CH4

(b) The blue zone of the flame is a region of complete combustion
in which the methane burns in oxygen to produce carbon
dioxide and water vapour. Write a word equation and a
balanced formula equation for this combustion reaction.
Methane + oxygen  carbon dioxide + water
CH4 + 2O2  CO2 + 2H2O

(c) A yellow safety flame is produced by closing the air hole.
Explain why the flame turns yellow.
The methane burns poorly (incomplete combustion) due to
a lower air supply. The flame turns yellow due to the soot
(carbon) particles in the flame.

To recycle or to not recycle
Greywater is wastewater generated from washing dishes, laundry and bathing in homes. It makes up
50–80 per cent of residential wastewater. Greywater does not contain chemical and biological
contaminants. Greywater gets its name from its cloudy appearance and from its status as being
neither fresh (whitewater from groundwater or taps) nor heavily polluted (blackwater).
If collected via a separate plumbing system, greywater can be recycled directly within the home
and garden. Recycled greywater of this kind is never clean enough to drink, but a number of stages
of filtration and microbial digestion can be used to provide water for washing or flushing toilets;
relatively clean greywater may be applied directly from the sink to the garden, because it receives
treatment from the soil and plant roots. Vegetables should not be watered with greywater.
On 26 July 2006, 61.62 per cent of Toowoomba’s residents opposed the treating of sewage for
drinking water. Under the plan, wastewater would have been collected and put through a series of
purifying treatments, including ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis and oxidation. The treated water would

searchText:
CHAPTER 6: Inside the atom

Worksheet 6.2
Science Quest 9: pages 240–1

How big is an atom?
Answers
It is hard to visualise the size of tiny objects, like atoms and their nuclei. However, making
comparisons with something we are more familiar with sometimes helps.
Use an everyday object to create an image that will help people to understand how small the
nucleus of an atom is compared with the size of the entire atom. Choose from the suggestions
provided or use your own ideas. Atoms vary in size, but for the purpose of this activity, assume the
nucleus of an atom is 100 000 times smaller than the size of the entire atom.
(a) If a marshmallow represents the nucleus of an atom, how big would the entire atom be? (Hint:
You will need to measure the diameter or the length of a marshmallow.)
Marshmallows vary in size. In this calculation, the marshmallow is 3 cm long. If the nucleus is
3 cm on this scale, then the entire atom is 100 000 times larger.
 3  100 000
 300 000 cm
 3000 m
 3 km

(b) If one gradation on millimetre-lined A4 graph paper represents the nucleus of an atom, how
many sheets of graph paper would you need to glue together to represent the entire atom?
If the nucleus is 1 mm, then the diameter of the whole atom would be:
 1  100 000
 100 000 mm
 100 m.
A sheet of A4 graph paper is 25 cm long, which is 0.25 m.
Since 100 ÷ 0.25 = 400, 400 sheets of A4 graph paper would need to be glued together to
represent the size of the atom.

(c) If a marble, representing a nucleus, is placed in the centre of a sports ground, how big would the
sports ground need to be to represent the entire atom?

© Photodisc, Inc

If the marble nucleus has a diameter of 15 mm, then the diameter of the sports ground is
100 000 times the marble’s diameter.
 15  100 000
 1 500 000 mm
 1500 m
 1.5 km
Therefore, the sports ground would need to have a diameter of 1.5 km.

Stars that have a mass between one solar mass and eight solar masses will evolve into red giant
stars. Betelgeuse in the Orion constellation is a red giant star. During their lives, stars like our
sun, fuse hydrogen atoms together to form helium. Since helium is denser than hydrogen, the

searchText:
Worksheet 7.1

Nature’s time machine
Answers
Secrets in the ice
Scientists may not have discovered a time machine yet, but they do have
a way of looking back over 300 000 years by looking at ice cores.
Scientists drill into the ice of Antarctica and collect samples from deep
down. Ice cores provide information about the Earth and the atmosphere
over hundreds of thousands of years.
For thousands of years, snow has fallen in Antarctica. The snow
turns to ice, which builds up over time. Dust, gases and other
substances from the air become trapped. The trapped substances
provide information about what was in the air at the time the snow fell.
By studying dust in the ice cores, scientists can work out when
certain volcanoes have erupted. They have linked radioactive
substances in the ice to nuclear disasters in various parts of the world.
The dust and radioactive substances were probably carried to Antarctica
by the wind.
Scientists have used ice cores to track the amount of carbon
dioxide in the air and the Earth’s temperature. The graphs on this page
show how these have changed over the past 400 000 years.

Zero on the temperature scale represents the Earth’s average
temperature now. On the temperature line, the peaks
represent warmer periods of time. In between the peaks, the
average air temperature was up to 6°C lower than now. These
colder times are called the ice ages.

This ice core was drilled from
more than 3.7 km down. Parts of
it are more than 150 000 years
old. Photo: Public domain

The line for carbon dioxide resembles the temperature line.
When the temperature was higher, there was more carbon
dioxide in the air. When the temperature dropped, so did the
amount of carbon dioxide. (ppm means parts per million.)

Look at the graphs above of how carbon dioxide and temperature have changed over time and answer
the following questions.
1. How many ice ages have there been in the past 400 000 years? 4
2. At a point 350 000 years ago:
(a) how much carbon dioxide was in the air 200 ppm
(b) how much colder was the Earth’s air compared to the present temperature? 5 °C colder
3. Has the Earth ever been warmer than it is now? If so, how much warmer?
Yes, approximately 0.5 degrees warmer........................................................................................
4. When was the amount of carbon dioxide in the air the highest? Over 400 000 years ago..............
5. Why is an ice core like a time machine? Ice cores store the gases of the air so the conditions
can be studied.

© John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd

 Worksheet 7.1
Page 2

Recycling carbon
Carbon atoms are found in the air, soil, rocks, oil and gas below the Earth’s surface, and all living
things. The number of carbon atoms on Earth always remains the same. When living things use carbon
atoms, the atoms don’t just disappear; they are recycled. The diagram below shows the recycling of
carbon. It also shows how humans have added to the amount of carbon dioxide in the air. We must take
care not to interfere with the natural recycling process.
1. How do animals get carbon as part of the carbon cycle?

By eating plants and other animals
2. Explain two ways in which carbon that is contained within a plant can end up back in the air.
Respiration and decomposing
3. Where in the carbon cycle is carbon stored for long periods of time?

© John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd

 Underground as coal, oil or gas
4. Would the carbon cycle still take place if humans did not exist? Explain.
Yes, animals would play the part that humans play in the carbon cycle.
5. How do humans add extra carbon dioxide to the air?
By burning fossil fuel

Campsite chillout

Even while relaxing on holiday,

1. For each of the activities

listed below, state whether the
process indicated is
exothermic or endothermic,
and then explain your choices.
(Remember: an exothermic
process results in thermal
energy being given out to the
surroundings, while an
endothermic process requires
thermal energy which is
drawn in from the
surroundings.)
(a) The leaves use energy from the sun to make sugars for the tree (photosynthesis).
Endothermic — energy is being absorbed.

(b) Nuclear reactions in the sun warm the Earth during the day.
Exothermic — energy is being released.

(c) Sweat on a person's face evaporates.
Endothermic — energy is being absorbed. Change of state: liquid  gas.

(d) The gas barbecue burns.
Exothermic — energy is being released

(e) The eggs inside the saucepan cook to become hard-boiled.
Endothermic — energy is being absorbed

(f) Glasses fog up from the boiling water.
Exothermic — energy is being released. Change of state: gas  liquid.

(g) Insect repellent is liquid inside the can, partly gaseous as it comes out of the nozzle.
Endothermic — energy is being absorbed. Change of state: liquid  gas.

(h) Ice melts in a drink.
Endothermic — energy is being absorbed. Change of state: solid  liquid.

2. Which of these processes can be classified as chemical reactions? Explain your choices fully.
Chemical reactions are irreversible and involve the formation of a new substance.
(a) Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water  glucose + oxygen
(b) This is an example of a nuclear reaction in which the internal structure of the atom changes
and different types of atoms are formed.
(d) Combustion of methane: methane + oxygen  carbon dioxide + water
(e) The proteins in the egg change (denature and coagulate). This is irreversible.

title: Worksheet 7.5 - Slowing Global Warming - Alternatives (Answers)
subject: Science
searchText:
Worksheet 7.5

Slowing global
warming — alternatives
Answers
Wind power
The wind is free and blows almost continuously; a series of wind
turbines can supply a viable and reliable source of energy. It has the
added advantage of being non-polluting. However, there has been
controversy as wind farms can be quite noisy and some people think
they spoil the aesthetics of the natural environment.

Photo: chuyu / 123RF

Nuclear power
Australia has vast reserves of uranium, the essential element
required to produce nuclear power. Enormous amounts of energy
can be harnessed through nuclear power generation, but the risks
are also great. Waste products and spent nuclear rods remain
radioactive for thousands of years, and if a reactor goes into
‘meltdown’ or these waste materials leak into the environment, the
results could be devastating.
Photo: hxdyl / 123RF

Hydro-electric power
Hydro-electricity has been used for decades as an important
source of electricity. The natural force of running water
turns massive turbines, which produces electricity cheaply.
It is also non-polluting. However, river systems must be
dammed and this affects the natural environment. Larger
tracts of land are often flooded in the process, resulting in
the destruction of habitats.
Photo: Amornthep Chotchuang / 123RF

© John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd

 Worksheet 7.5

Biosphere 2
More than three decades ago, scientists first raised concerns that the Earth was heading for an
‘ecological meltdown’. Their solution was a project known as Biosphere 2. The aim was to replicate the
various ecosystems on the Earth, as well as its atmosphere, in a series of domes occupying
approximately 1.3 hectares.
In 1991 the project reached fruition, when four men and four women took up residence within the
facility for two years. The project was plagued with problems, including the collapse of ecosystems and
the demise of several plant and animal species. However, a more serious problem was the inability to
sustain an atmosphere; falling oxygen levels and rising
carbon dioxide levels meant the project was doomed to fail
without external assistance.
Perhaps what scientists really gained was an insight into
our future. If we continue to rely on fossil fuels, our climate
will continue to change and the atmosphere will continue to
deteriorate. We will not simply be able to prop it up from
another source. Alternative power sources such as
hydroelectricity, wind and nuclear energy are considered
sustainable, if somewhat controversial.
Photo: James Mattil / 123RF
1. Explain what is meant by the term ‘ecological meltdown’.
An ecological meltdown means that the ecology of the planet would be changed by increasing
temperatures.

2. What was the aim of Biosphere 2?
To replicate various ecosystems on Earth as well as its atmosphere

3. What important lessons do you think we can learn from the Biosphere 2 project? Justify your
answer.
That it is difficult to sustain an atmosphere without external help and that the future will look
different for the production of energy

title: Worksheet 9.2 - Science under scrutiny
subject: Science
searchText:
Worksheet 9.2

Science under scrutiny
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class: ................................................

Scientists and their discoveries do not inhabit an isolated world. Some scientific discoveries can be
detrimental to different factions within the community. Many of these groups have a great deal of
influence over what people think about a scientific issue or even over the funding of the scientific work
itself. Read the following two examples of science and society not always being in absolute agreement.

Smokescreen
The viewpoint of the tobacco industry — that it
needs to make profits to remain in business — is
quite different to that of the scientists who
discovered the link between tobacco smoking and
disease. Early last century, smoking was an
acceptable social habit. However, as scientists
started to gather evidence of its link with heart
disease and lung cancer, people started to
examine the value of smoking and to consider
the dangers for non-smokers who breathe
others’ cigarette smoke.
In 1964, doctors in the United States issued
the first official warning about the health
hazards of smoking, based on the results of
their research. This scientific evidence was
extremely damaging to the very large tobacco
industry and they opposed it with research of
their own.
Some people believe that the tobacco
industry should pay the public health bills of
those suffering the ill effects of smoking. This
debate continues, but society no longer accepts
that smokers have the right to smoke in many
public places. Laws have been passed that
prohibit smoking in all enclosed public areas,
including offices and most motel rooms. Tobacco
advertising has been banned in the Australian
media. Millions of dollars have been spent
educating people about the risks of smoking,
fighting legal compensation battles and
establishing laws.
Despite this, it is only in recent years that
some parts of the tobacco industry have admitted
the link between tobacco smoking and disease,
and that the nicotine in tobacco is addictive.

Pill poppers
Another example is the overuse of antibiotics, the
chemicals that are used to kill disease-causing
microbes. It is a fact that, although more people
were injured in World War II than World War I,
fewer died. This was due to the discovery and
development of antibiotics between the wars —
their availability during World War II saved
many lives. Despite
the great advantages
of antibiotics, we
now know that their
overuse can cause an
increase in the
numbers of resistant
microbes (that is,
microbes that cannot
be killed by the
antibiotics). The
drug companies that
market antibiotics
want to encourage
increased sales of their drugs. Some patients are
in the habit of taking medicine for any ailment,
and doctors write prescriptions so that they do not
appear negligent.
However, overuse of antibiotics can result in
people dying from diseases that could have been
cured by antibiotics in the past, but for which the
drugs have lost their effect. This product of
science has amazing benefits to society, yet it can
lead to negative effects if not properly used. It is
up to us to be responsible and take antibiotics
only when they are strictly necessary, so that they
can continue to be effective in future.

1. Why was the tobacco industry so reluctant to agree with the scientific findings about the serious
effects of smoking on people’s health?

CHAPTER 5: Chemical reactions

Worksheet 5.6

Corrosion and combustion
Answers
Corrosion
1. Corrosion is a process in which a metal or alloy is attacked by agents such as air and water,
leading to the degradation and destruction of the material. The following diagrams compare the
corrosion of iron and aluminium.
(a) As both metals are attacked, oxide layers form on the
surface. The iron oxide is called rust. Use your
knowledge of the activity series of metals to predict
which metal (Fe or Al) will react with air and water
more rapidly.
Al as it is higher in the activity series than Fe.

(b) Iron continues to rust whereas aluminium stops
corroding. Explain why this happens.
The iron oxide (rust) layer is porous. Oxygen and
water continue to penetrate through the rust layer to
attack the iron beneath. This does not happen with
aluminium oxide as the corrosion layer on the surface
is non-porous.

(c) Name a metal that is used to coat iron to prevent it from rusting.
Zinc (process = galvanising)
.................................................................................................................................................

Combustion
2. In combustion reactions a substance reacts with oxygen and releases energy. The energy
released can be in the form of heat, light and sometimes sound. The following diagram shows
the blue flame of a Bunsen burner.
(a) The Bunsen burner uses natural gas, which is mainly
methane. Write the chemical formula for methane.
CH4

(b) The blue zone of the flame is a region of complete combustion
in which the methane burns in oxygen to produce carbon
dioxide and water vapour. Write a word equation and a
balanced formula equation for this combustion reaction.
Methane + oxygen  carbon dioxide + water
CH4 + 2O2  CO2 + 2H2O

(c) A yellow safety flame is produced by closing the air hole.
Explain why the flame turns yellow.
The methane burns poorly (incomplete combustion) due to
a lower air supply. The flame turns yellow due to the soot
(carbon) particles in the flame.

A huge variety of amazing creatures live in our oceans. Imagine you have been invited on board a
submersible craft that is capable of exploring the sea floor thousands of metres below the ocean
surface. As you descend, what changes will you observe in the animals and plants that inhabit the
ocean? Using the diagram above as a guide, write a brief description of how the plants and animals
change along your journey to the seabed. Think about the size, shape, colour and variety of
organisms at different depths. Write your descriptions in the table.
Changes observed in animals

As we travel deeper into the ocean, animals show adaptations for life in darkness, cold water and
high pressure. Many of the animals would have large eyes, helping them see in the dark waters.
Some will be small, dark and thin to help camouflage them. Other animals will glow in the dark.
Because there is less plant food, animals in the ocean depths will not be as active because they
have less energy available. Carnivores may have large mouths and jaws to capture prey with less
energy expenditure. Once we get past the ‘twilight zone’, animals may not have eyes at all as there
is no light this far down. Most animals at this depth will be invertebrates due to high water pressure.

is into three groups: carnivore; omnivore and herbivore. Write the term

Bears in Canada are often photographed
catching fish as the fish try to jump up
waterfalls on their way to breed upstream.
Bears are also seen picking berries from low
bushes. Campers have to place all their food
and rubbish in sealed containers or bears will
steal it from them.
There are many different goannas and their
diets vary. Their prey includes insects, snakes,
smaller lizards, birds and birds’ eggs. Some
giant goannas will kill a young kangaroo or
even attack a dog. Goannas are attracted by
the smell of rotting meat and feed off the
bodies of dead animals.
Desert hopping mice live in very harsh
environments with little rain. To survive they
have to eat what is available to them and have
a varied diet of seeds, leaves, shoots, roots
and insects.
The common brushtail possum has adapted
to living in cities and suburbs. In its natural
habitat a brushtail possum eats mainly leaves
and flowers. A particular favourite is fresh gum
tips. Possums occasionally eat insects, eggs
and meat. In urban areas they hunt through
open compost bins to see what they can find.
Dugongs are large sea creatures that feed on
sea-grass beds on the bottom of the ocean
floor. They use their flippers to uproot the seagrasses and then the dugongs chew and crush
their food. If sea grasses are not available,
dugongs will eat algae. Scientific studies have
identified the remains of worms and shellfish in
the waste produced by dugongs. Scientists are
not sure if these are eaten accidentally with the
sea grasses or if the dugongs eat them
intentionally.
The diet of yellow-footed rock wallabies is
similar to most other wallabies. They eat grass,
plants and shrubs, which they chew with flat
teeth at the back of their jaw.
